At the same time, we recognise that the transition to electric mobility requires much more than launching a vehicle. Building customer 
confidence requires the creation of a reliable and convenient ecosystem around EV ownership. Accordingly, we continue to strengthen 
EV readiness across our ecosystem through an expanding charging infrastructure, EV-ready service workshops and partnerships with 
charge point operators. Our focus remains on making electric mobility practical, convenient and accessible to customers
However, for a country as large and diverse as India, no single technology pathway can adequately address all mobility needs.
Therefore, our approach remains centered around a multi-pathway strategy comprising Battery Electric Vehicles, Strong Hybrid Electric 
Vehicles, CNG, Compressed Biogas (CBG), E20-compatible vehicles and Flex Fuel technologies. We believe such an approach offers 
the most practical pathway towards carbon reduction while preserving affordability, customer choice, energy security and suitability to 
local conditions. By pursuing multi-powertrain approach, we could achieve our CAFE (Phase-2) target for FY 2025-26 by a good margin.
Among these pathways, I am excited about the opportunities presented by biofuels and Compressed Biogas (CBG) in particular.
India possesses abundant biomass resources, creating a significant opportunity to produce low-carbon fuel domestically. Beyond 
reducing

emissions, CBG has the potential to simultaneously strengthen energy atmanirbharta by reducing dependence on imported 
fossil fuels and supply chain atmanirbharta by creating local value chains and supporting rural economy. CBG also helps to improve air 
quality in urban areas as it uses paddy straw as a feedstock, thereby reducing crop burning. The increasing importance being accorded 
to biogas, including during recent engagements between the Prime Ministers of India and Japan, reinforces its strategic relevance for 
the future.
Technology is also transforming the Company in ways that go well beyond vehicle powertrains.
The rapid rise of software content in vehicles and the advances being made in Artificial Intelligence, particularly Generative AI, are 
fundamentally reshaping product development, manufacturing, quality management, safety improvement and customer experience. 
As we scale up, digital technologies are becoming indispensable for improving efficiency, enabling faster and more informed decision-
making, and enhancing organisational agility. Across Maruti Suzuki, we are increasingly leveraging digital technologies. 
As we embrace these opportunities, we remain conscious of emerging risks.
The automotive industry today operates not only in a more interconnected but also more uncertain world. The increasing adoption 
of advanced technologies is also leading to greater dependence on specialised materials, semiconductors, batteries and electronic 
components, supply chains for which remain concentrated in a limited number of countries.
Recent geopolitical developments, including the conflict in West Asia, have highlighted the vulnerability of global supply chains and 
reinforced the need to balance efficiency with resilience.
Localisation, alternate sourcing, supplier capability development and ecosystem development remain critical priorities. Our objective 
is not merely to mitigate risk but to strengthen India's long-term competitiveness in future mobilit

y technologies.
Sustainability remains integral to our business strategy.
For us, sustainability is not a separate agenda. It is embedded in the way we design products, operate factories, manage resources 
and engage with stakeholders. Our efforts span the entire vehicle lifecycle, from product development and manufacturing to logistics, 
usage and end-of-life management.
We continue to improve resource efficiency and reduce energy demand by adopting Suzuki’s core philosophy of Sho-Sho-Kei-Tan-Bi, 
which translates to smaller, lighter, fewer, shorter and more beautiful.  At the same time, we are transitioning towards clean energy driven 
by renewable electricity and increasing use of biogas as a process fuel. The Company has plans to expand capacity of solar power 
generation from 79.2 MWp to 319 MWp by FY 2030-31. Besides, to maximise the use of renewable power we procure green power from 
external sources and use Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) having a capacity of 1 MWh. By 2027, capacity of in-plant biogas plant 
will increase to 10.7 TPD from 0.7 TPD.  The Company continues to increasingly adopt rail-based logistics to reduce logistics-related 
emissions. 
During the year, the Company further strengthened ESG practices across its value chain by promoting renewable energy adoption, 
responsible sourcing and robust governance standards among suppliers and dealer partners. It also continued to enforce global 
standards on the management of Substances of Concern (SoC), conducting over 470 supplier assessments and awareness programmes 
to drive compliance and capability enhancement.
The Company remains committed to building a responsible and resilient value chain. Cumulatively, human resource systems and 
human rights practices were assessed for local Tier-1 suppliers accounting for 84% of component purchases by value. In addition, the 
Company continued to promote occupational health and safety, skill development and governance excellence across its ecosystem.

During FY 2025–26, over 2,550 training programmes were conducted covering 100% of Tier-1 suppliers and dealer partners, while a 
comprehensive governance framework was extended across all Tier-1 suppliers to strengthen transparency, risk management, ethical 
conduct and sustainable value creation.
One of the greatest strengths of Maruti Suzuki is its culture of partnership and participation. The growth of our employees and the growth 
of the Company have always been intrinsically linked. During FY 2025–26, employees contributed more than 1.8 million suggestions 
aimed at improving safety, quality, productivity and cost competitiveness. This remarkable achievement reflects a deeply embedded 
culture of ownership, continuous improvement and shared success.
With pace of technological change accelerating and workforce getting younger, preserving the values and culture that have shaped our 
success while building future-ready capabilities remains a strategic priority. The technologies of the future can be acquired and developed. 
Values and culture take decades to build. Sustaining these foundations while preparing the organisation for future opportunities will 
remain one of our most important responsibilities.
The CSR initiatives continue to progress as guided by the Board. Through the CSR programmes, the Company continues to create a 
positive impact on the lives of the people in the areas of community development, road safety and skill development. 
The Company undertakes community development initiatives near its facilities, focusing on healthcare, education, sanitation, and 
infrastructure. Its multispecialty hospital and Podar Learn School in Sitapur, Gujarat, both in their fifth year of operation, have served 
over 150,000 patients and provided quality education to local students. The Fermented Organic Manure (FOM) initiative, undertaken in 
collaboration with agricultural and research institutions, expanded across nine states to evaluate its potential and prom

ote sustainable 
farming practices among over 200,000 farmers.
On road safety, the Company has trained over 5.5 million people over the last 25 years and established 86 automated driving test tracks 
in partnership with the transport departments of Uttar Pradesh, Delhi, Uttarakhand, Bihar, Haryana, Jammu & Kashmir, Rajasthan, 
Chhattisgarh, Andhra Pradesh and Tamil Nadu. These tracks use computer vision systems and AI-based technology to assess driving 
skills transparently and efficiently before the issuance of driving licenses.
In skill development, the Company is working towards creating livelihood opportunities for Indian youth by imparting training in relevant 
skills through the Japan India Institutes for Manufacturing (JIM) set up by the Company and by supporting 144 Industrial Training Institutes 
(ITIs) nationwide. Over 19,600 students were trained in FY 2025-26. This programme aligns with the Government of India’s Skill India 
initiative.
Finally, as India progresses towards becoming a developed nation by 2047, the automobile industry has both a responsibility and 
an opportunity to contribute meaningfully to this journey. Through manufacturing, exports, technology development, employment 
generation, skill creation and sustainable mobility, Maruti Suzuki remains committed to supporting India's aspirations.
The next million vehicles represent far more than a volume milestone. They represent greater access to mobility, stronger manufacturing 
capabilities, wider adoption of cleaner technologies, deeper localisation and broader value creation for society.
I firmly believe that the momentum created during FY 2025–26 positions us well for the opportunities ahead.
I would like to express my sincere gratitude to our shareholders, customers, employees, suppliers, dealers, logistics partners, government 
authorities and all other stakeholders for their continued trust and support.
Together, we will continue our efforts to expand the Joy of Mobility and create sust

ainable value for society and future generations.

The Company marked its entry into the Battery Electric Vehicle 
(BEV) segment in India with the introduction of the e VITARA in 
FY 2025-26. The e VITARA is Suzuki Motor Corporation’s first BEV 
offering, and the Company will serve as the global manufacturing

Broad Overview of Biogas Production at Manesar Facility
B. Increasing Use of Renewable Process Fuels
Use of Biofuel – Generating Compressed Biogas from Food Waste
The Company undertook initiatives in FY 2025-26 to increase the 
capacity of the biogas plant at its Manesar facility. In FY 2024-25, 
the Company had set up a pilot biogas project at Manesar using 
in-house food waste and Napier grass as resources.
The pilot project had a capacity of 0.2 Tonnes Per Day (TPD) that 
was scaled up to 0.7 TPD in FY 2025-26, marking another step in 
the Company’s commitment to sustainable manufacturing.
The Company is in process of setting up a 10 TPD biogas plant 
at its Kharkhoda facility, which is expected to be commissioned 
by 2027.
Aligned with the Government’s broader ‘waste to wealth’ 
philosophy, the facility utilises paddy straw as feedstock, 
with a provision to enhance output through the use of cattle 
dung. It leverages anaerobic digestion technology to convert 
agricultural waste into raw biogas. The plant is expected to 
generate approximately 2.6 lakh standard cubic metres of biogas 
annually, resulting in an estimated avoidance of 474 tonnes of CO₂ 
emissions per year.
The plant’s biogas can be utilised in paint shop heating processes 
as well as in canteen operations. Fermented Organic Manure 
(FOM), a by-product of the process, will be used for internal 
horticulture or supplied back to the agricultural ecosystem.

to have railway siding facilities, currently operational at two of its

rail-based vehicle dispatches was achieved in just 21 months,

based vehicle dispatches to 35% by FY 2030-31. Leveraging the 
efficiency of rail transport, the in-plant railway sidings help reduce 
the carbon footprint of logistics operations while also easing road 
congestion and lowering overall fuel consumption.

External Environment
External Environment
Strategic Response
The Company continues to pursue a multi-powertrain 
strategy comprising BEVs, SHEVs, CNG, Compressed 
Biogas (CBG) and ethanol-compatible vehicles. The 
Company believes a multi-pathway decarbonisation 
approach will maximise carbon reduction, enable 
customers to choose solutions best suited to their needs, 
diversify technology risks and support long-term business 
resilience and financial health.
Recognising that product use accounts for the majority 
of a vehicle'

s lifecycle emissions, the Company remains 
focused on reducing emissions through multiple powertrain 
technologies. At the same time, it is pursuing greenhouse 
gas reduction opportunities across the value chain, 
including manufacturing operations, energy consumption, 
logistics and the supplier ecosystem. 
India's economy remained resilient during FY 2025-26, 
despite geopolitical uncertainty, trade disruptions and 
commodity volatility.  GST reduction on cars improved 
affordability and revived participation from first-time 
buyers, particularly in the small car segment, a key driver 
of sustained industry growth.
Geopolitical developments continue to create uncertainty 
around commodity prices, energy costs, logistics networks 
and supply chain stability. Besides, geopolitical tensions 
and the emergence of tariff barriers pose risks to global 
trade and market access. 
Increasing acceptance of India-manufactured vehicles 
and recently concluded Free Trade Agreements (FTAs) 
with key markets such as the UK and EU are creating new 
opportunities for automotive exports. These developments 
are strengthening India's position as a global automotive 
manufacturing hub and expanding the growth potential of 
the automotive industry. 
India's low passenger vehicle penetration, rising incomes 
and increasing aspirations for personal mobility continue 
to provide substantial growth opportunities for the industry. 
Climate change continues to reshape the automotive 
industry globally. The pace and nature of the mobility 
transition is expected to vary across markets depending 
on economic conditions, infrastructure readiness and 
resource availability.
Several emerging powertrain technologies are yet to 
achieve the level of cost competitiveness required for 
widespread adoption in a price-sensitive market such 
as India. In addition, supply chains for certain critical 
materials remain concentrated, creating potential cost and 
availability risks.
For India, balancing ca

rbon reduction with affordability, 
accessibility and suitability to local resource conditions 
remains critical. Consequently, Battery Electric Vehicles 
(BEVs), Strong Hybrid Electric Vehicles (SHEVs), CNG, 
biofuels and other low-carbon technologies are expected 
to complement one another in reducing emissions. 
The global automotive industry is undergoing a once-in-
a-century transformation, resulting in a rapidly evolving 
regulatory landscape. Accordingly, the regulatory 
environment in India is shaping up.
Given the breadth of the Company's product portfolio and 
powertrain offerings, regulatory compliance is resource-
intensive. The sudden regulatory changes and non-tariff 
barriers have the potential to influence market access and 
export competitiveness. 
India's growing importance as the world's third-largest 
passenger vehicle market is expected to intensify competition 
and accelerate innovation across the industry.
With annual passenger vehicle sales approaching 5 million 
units, India has emerged as one of the world's most important 
automotive markets. Continued economic growth, rising 
incomes and favourable demographic trends are expected 
to further enhance its attractiveness for both domestic and 
global automotive players. 
Importantly, the Company believes that a changing 
competitive landscape ultimately benefits customers 
by driving innovation, improving product offerings and 
enhancing overall value. 
Strategic Response
To mitigate near-term risks, the Company continues to 
focus on cost optimisation, localisation, strengthening 
supply chain resilience, developing alternate sources of 
supply and expanding its supplier base.
Reflecting confidence in long-term domestic and 
export opportunities, the Company increased its annual 
production capacity from approximately 2.4 million units 
to 2.9 million units during FY 2026-27 and remains on 
course to achieve its medium-term objective of expanding 
annual production capacity to 4 million unit

s. Supported by 
Suzuki Motor Corporation's global network and diversified 
presence across international markets, exports are 
expected to remain an important pillar of the Company's 
long-term growth strategy. 
Strategic Response
Access to Suzuki Motor Corporation's technological 
capabilities remains a critical enabler for timely regulatory 
compliance across domestic and international markets. 
Simultaneously, the Company continues to strengthen 
its engineering, testing and regulatory preparedness 
capabilities through investments in advanced infrastructure 
and the Rohtak R&D facility. These efforts enhance its 
ability to meet evolving regulations while continuing 
to deliver safe, efficient and technologically advanced 
mobility solutions.
Strategic Response
The Company continues to strengthen its competitiveness 
through product portfolio expansion, localisation, 
manufacturing excellence and access to advanced 
technologies through Suzuki Motor Corporation. Ongoing 
investments in product development, safety, quality and 
customer experience are aimed at sustaining long-term 
competitiveness in an evolving market environment.

Risk Management
The Company understands that effective risk management is critical in meeting its strategic objectives and achieving sustainable 
growth. It has a structured risk management process, which is overseen by the Risk Management Committee. This Committee 
monitors and reviews the Company’s risk management plan as per relevant provisions of the Companies Act, 2013, and Listing 
Regulations. Accountability for the mitigation of each risk is assigned to the identified risk owners.
The Company applied the net risk principle to determine its risks. The top management monitors mitigation measures to counter 
these risks. If the following risks manifest, they have negative implications.
Mitigation Measures
•	 Maintaining close communication with suppliers
•	 Strengthening supplier capabilities and improving their 
resilience
•	 Diversification of procurement source - Alternate 
suppliers/locations
•	 Enhanced focus on localisation
•	 Temporary increase in the inventory of components
•	 Use of advanced technologies for prevention and 
quick suppression of fire

Providing Vocational Training to Youth
•	 The Company supports 144 Industrial Training Institutes (ITIs) 
nationwide that have imparted vocational training to around 
19,400 students so far.
•	 The Company installed high voltage (EV and SHEVs) training 
equipment in 130 ITIs. Through this facility, more than 2,700

•	 The Company also started four Japan India Institutes for 
Manufacturing (JIM) — two in Gujarat and the other two in 
Haryana. These institutes are the result of a collaboration 
between the governments of Japan and India to create a

Circularity Management
In a first-of-its-kind initiative to transition from a linear to circular 
material flow model, Maruti Suzuki has operationalised a 
closed-loop material circularity framework for ferrous (Steel) 
and non-ferrous (Aluminium) scrap generated at its plants. The 
Company's closed-loop model strengthens material circularity 
and contributes to emissions reduction.
Material Circularity 
Supply chain operations are one of the major contributors 
to the Company’s overall GHG emissions (Scope 3.1). Steel 
and aluminium are the two major materials. Therefore, 
decarbonisation of the supply chain remains a key enabler in the 
Company’s journey towards Carbon Neutrality.
Steel scrap and aluminium scrap generated during vehicle 
manufacturing are routed to approved raw material suppliers 
for recycling into alloy steel grades and aluminium ingots, thus 
establishing a closed-loop circularity system. This initiative is 
estimated to reduce GHG emissions with steel and aluminium 
recycling through logistics optimisation to reduce dependency 
on imported scrap.
Benefits of Material Circularity
1.	 Resource Efficiency: Internal reuse of scrap 
from press, casting and machining shops reduces 
dependency on virgin and imported raw materials
2.	 Raw Material Security: Closed-loop local 
recycling secures a consistent supply of recycled 
metal, reducing vulnerability to global supply chain 
disruptions
3.	 GHG Emission Reduction: Supply chain 
optimisation through scrap circularity reduces 
greenhouse gas emissions across the value chain

Environmental Sustainability in Products
As a responsible manufacturer, the Company remains at the forefront of India's passenger vehicle market. The Company continues to 
drive innovation and demonstrate strategic agility in areas such as electrification, sustainability, carbon neutrality, and next-generation 
mobility solutions, while responding to intensifying competition from both domestic and global players.
New Products
The Company continues to pursue a multi-powertrain strategy 
comprising BEVs, SHEVs, CNG, Compressed Biogas (CBG) 
and ethanol-compatible vehicles. The Company believes a 
multi-pathway decarbonisation approach will maximise carbon 
reduction, enable customers to choose solutions best suited to 
their needs and diversify technology risks. 
Introducing Battery Electric Vehicles (BEV)
The Company launched an electric SUV - e VITARA marking a 
transformative milestone in India’s electric mobility journey. The 
Company is expected to launch four EV models by FY 2030-
31. The Company is working to create a robust electric vehicle 
ecosystem with comprehensive end-to-end digital platform, the 
‘e for Me’ app, for EV charging needs, including home charging 
and public charging with an integrated payment journey. Over 
2000 exclusive charging points will be available to customers 
acro

ss the nationwide dealer network. The Company will work 
with partners to enable over 100,000 public charging points by 
2030.
CNG
Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) remains a key environment-
friendly pillar in the Company’s  mobility portfolio, offering its 
customers a lower-emissions transportation alternative with 
enhanced fuel economy that incurs lower operating cost. The 
Company currently offers CNG technology across 14 models 
and commands nearly three-fourths of the market share of CNG 
vehicles in the industry.
Hybrid
In parallel, the Company continues to promote its Hybrid 
technology portfolio by offering Smart Hybrid (Mild Hybrid) and 
Strong Hybrid. Smart Hybrid Technology enhances fuel efficiency 
and reduces dependence on conventional IC engines through 
electric motor assistance whereas, Strong Hybrid engines enable 
switching to an electric-only driving mode contributing to lower 
tailpipe emissions.
CBG
The Company is committed to explore sustainable mobility, 
Maruti Suzuki continues to advance a multi-pathway approach 
toward reducing carbon emissions. Recognising the significant 
potential of Compressed Bio-Gas (CBG) in India's energy 
transition, the Company has identified CBG as a strategic fuel that 
complements its strong CNG vehicle portfolio while supporting 
the Company's overall environmental objectives.
The Company continues to evaluate advancements in flex-fuel 
vehicle technology to support cleaner and more sustainable 
mobility solutions.
Designed for End-of-Life
The Company vehicles are designed in accordance with the 
minimum 85% Recyclability and 95% Recoverability requirements 
calculated through International Material Data System (IMDS) 
following ISO 22628, to assess material composition and 
end-of-life performance, thereby supporting responsible 
resource recovery. The average recyclability for the products 
manufactured by the Company is 92% and recoverability is 95%.
The Company also shared its perspective on reducing greenhou

se gas emissions within India's passenger car sector, 
introducing the 'Clean for Life Vehicles' (CLV) concept as part of the GHG reduction framework.

Japan India Institute for Manufacturing 
Japan India Institute for Manufacturing (JIM) is a flagship skill 
development initiative that offers vocational training aligned with 
advanced manufacturing requirements. It reflects the collaborative 
efforts

between the Governments of India and Japan to promote 
skill development and excellence in the manufacturing sector. 
During the reporting period, over 300 students were trained 
across JIMs, taking the cumulative number to approximately 
2,300+ students since inception. Through short-term courses, 
over 2,800 individuals were trained during the reporting period. 
The Company has established four JIMs - two in Gujarat and two 
in Haryana, with JIM Sonipat commencing admissions for its first 
batch during the reporting period. The overall capacity of JIMs was 
further enhanced to accommodate a larger number of students.
JIMs are affiliated under NCVET (National Council for Vocational 
Education and Training) and accredited by the Ministry of Economy, 
trade and Industry (METI), Japan. JIMs follow the Dual System 
of Training (DST), combining classroom instruction with industry 
exposure. Students undergo seven months of paid industry 
training annually, enabling practical experience and 'Earn While 
You Learn' opportunities, thereby strengthening their transition 
to the workforce.
JIMs provide training in advanced manufacturing techniques and 
efficient shop floor practices based on Japanese manufacturing 
principles, along with essential soft skills to improve employability. 
The institutes are equipped with state‑of‑the‑art infrastructure, 
including mini‑vehicle assembly lines, engine assembly lines, 
safety labs, welding and painting simulators, full‑fledged paint 
booths, robotics‑enabled systems and body repair facilities. During 
the year, welding robots were installed at JIM Manesar and Sonipat 
and Electric Vehicle (EV) training equipment was introduced at JIM 
Mehsana, strengthening future‑ready skill development.
Infrastructure development continued with the start of construction 
of student hostel facilities at JIM Sonipat and Manesar to support 
residential training needs. JIMs achieved a 100% pass percentage, 
with six students securing state‑level top

ranks.

Compliance continues to be a fundamental pillar of Maruti 
Suzuki’s governance framework. The Company remains 
committed to maintaining a robust and forward-looking 
compliance architecture aligned with evolving regulatory 
expectations and leading industry practices. The Company had 
proactively benchmarked its Compliance practices with best-in-
class industry players and implemented additional Compliance 
initiatives to further strengthen its Compliance framework, 
including operationalising the Compliance Committee. During the 
year, this commitment was further reinforced through quarterly 
meetings of the Compliance Committee comprising of senior 
business and compliance leaders, chaired by the Managing 
Director and CEO, Mr. H. Takeuchi. The strengthened governance 
structure has enhanced oversight of compliance risks, improved 
visibility at the senior management level, and facilitated the timely 
and effective implementation of compliance initiatives across the 
organisation.
The seamless integration of Suzuki Motor Gujarat (SMG) into the 
Company’s operations has been executed with a strong focus on 
regulatory alignment and reinforcement of a unified compliance 
culture. The integration process ensured that SMG’s operations 
are fully aligned with the Company’s established governance 
framework, policies, and applicable regulatory requirements. 
Through structured oversight, harmonisation of controls, and 
targeted compliance trainings, the Company has embedded 
consistent standards of ethical conduct, risk management, and 
statutory c

ompliance across the integrated entity. This approach 
has strengthened overall compliance discipline, transparency, 
and accountability, while fostering a culture of integrity and 
adherence to regulatory expectations.
The Company is in full compliance with all applicable laws and 
regulations, including those governing labour, environmental, 
industrial, financial, IT, and corporate matters, as well as 
requirements under the Companies Act, 2013 and SEBI (Listing 
Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 as 
amended. Compliance certificates are submitted to the Board on 
a quarterly basis. To further strengthen monitoring and control, a 
Company-wide compliance e-monitoring tool was implemented 
during the reporting period. No significant instances of non-
compliance were reported during the year.
The Company marked its 10th Compliance Month in October 
2025, reaffirming its commitment to integrating compliance 
with business excellence. The Company continued to foster its 
culture of compliance through active leadership engagement, 
including participation by the Chairman, Mr. R C Bhargava, and 
the Managing Director and CEO, Mr. H. Takeuchi. This initiative 
was supported by structured awareness and training initiatives 
reinforcing compliance accountability across all levels of the 
organisation.
Extending its governance philosophy beyond the organisation, 
the Company enhanced its supplier engagement initiative through 
the 'Maruti Suzuki Supplier Corporate Governance Framework', 
aimed at promoting transparency, accountability, and adoption 
of corporate governance best practices across the value chain. 
The framework, co-developed with key suppliers, has already 
been adopted by 90% of its suppliers, reflecting the Company’s 
commitment to responsible and sustainable business practices.
Further, the Company conducted its second annual Compliance 
Survey (R 5.18) with full employee participation, enabling 
assessment of ground-level awarenes

s and implementation of 
compliance practices. The tone for this year's R 5.18 survey was 
set by MD and CEO, Mr. H. Takeuchi, by urging all employees to 
take the survey without any fear and report compliance concerns 
without hesitation. Insights from the survey have led to targeted 
interventions to strengthen the compliance framework and 
reinforce a culture of openness and continuous improvement.

Whistle Blower Mechanism
The Company’s Whistle Blower Policy establishes a robust 
mechanism for employees to report concerns relating to unethical 
conduct, violations of the Code of Business Conduct and Ethics 
(COBCE), or any other irregularities, in a secure and confidential 
manner. The framework ensures accessibility of reporting channels 
and safeguards against any form of retaliation.
Complaints may be raised directly with the designated 
Ombudsperson or through the Company’s Complaint Committee. All 
concerns received are treated with due seriousness and are subject 
to a structured, impartial, and time-bound investigation process. 
During the reporting period, two complaints were received by the 
Ombudsperson and were duly noted by the Audit Committee of the 
Board. Any matter received by the ombudsperson is investigated 
by the complaint committee with the support of an independent 
external expert to ensure objectivity and rigour, if required. Based 
on the findings, appropriate actions are taken in accordance with 
the Company’s Disciplinary Policy.

Competition Law
Case Related to After-market Sale of Spare Parts
An investigation was initiated by the Competition Commission of India (CCI) in 2011 against a few car manufacturing 
companies wherein it was contended that these companies were not making genuine spare parts of automobiles 
freely available in the open market. CCI later expanded the scope of the investigation to other car manufacturing 
companies, including the Company. In the final order passed by the CCI on 25th August 2014, certain directions 
were laid down against the automobile companies and penalties were imposed. A penalty of ₹4,711.4 million was 
imposed on the Company. 
The Company contested this matter before the Delhi High Court primarily on the ground that it was not a named 
party in the investigation and that the investigation ought not to have been conducted against the Company. On the 
contrary, the Company was named in the information given by the informant as a Company that made spare parts 
easily accessible in the open market. The Delhi High Court, on 16th May 2019, disposed of the petition stating that 
the Company had alternative remedies available. Thereafter, the Company filed a Special Leave Petition before the 
Supreme Court of India, wherein a stay o

n the CCI’s order was granted, and the stay is continuing.
Matter Relating to Discount Control Practices
An investigation was initiated suo-moto by the CCI in February 2019 based on the information provided by a purported 
dealer of the Company. The dealer alleged that the Company resorts to anti-competitive discount control practices. 
The CCI passed its final order on 23rd August 2021 and held that the Company indulged in anti-competitive discount 
control practices (resale price maintenance) and imposed a penalty of ₹2,000 million on the Company. The Company 
filed an appeal against the order of the CCI before the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLAT), wherein 
on 22nd November 2021, a stay on the order of the CCI was granted subject to the deposit of ₹200 million. The stay 
is continuing.

Information Security
Maruti Suzuki India Limited ('Maruti Suzuki') maintains a robust 
cyber security governance framework aligned with global 
standards and applicable regulatory requirements including 
the Information Technology (IT) Act, 2000. Guided by these 
requirements and international standards, the Company has 
established comprehensive information security policies, 
processes, and controls.
The Company is ISO 27001:2022 certified for Gurugram, 
Manesar, Head office, and Rohtak, with certification for the 
Kharkhoda and Hansalpur facilities successfully achieved during 
FY 2026-27. It operates under a comprehensive Information 
Security Management System (ISMS) Programme that governs 
cyber security risk management, data protection, and system 
resilience across the organisation.
The Company’

s Information Security policy provides management 
direction and guidance to ensure availability, integrity and 
confidentiality of information and information systems across 
locations. Management Information Security Forum (MISF) 
has been constituted and is chaired by Managing Director and 
comprises the Chief Information Security Officer (CISO) and 
other senior management personnel. The MISF facilitates internal 
communication of information security programs, implements 
processes for risk assessment and security classification of 
information systems and reports critical security matters to the 
Board of Directors. The company is working towards AIS 189/190 
compliance to meet regulatory requirements for automotive 
cybersecurity and software update management, thereby 
supporting vehicle safety and reliability.

The Company is committed to upholding the privacy rights of 
its stakeholders and ensuring the protection of personal data 
through responsible data governance practices. In compliance 
with applicable data protection laws, including the Information 
Technology Act, 2000 and the Digital Personal Data Protection

framework and associated controls. These initiatives are aimed 
at ensuring regulatory compliance, enhancing data security, and 
fostering stakeholder trust.

appointed a Data Protection Officer to manage the data privacy 
concerns. The Company has published the contact details of

ection policies and the evolving

hires and business advisories.

through these initiatives, reaffirming its commitment to personal 
data protection, regulatory compliance, and responsible

Maruti Suzuki India Limited works with a vast and diverse 
supplier ecosystem comprising over 450 Tier-1 suppliers

structured approach to enhance governance standards across

partners, launched the Supplier Corporate Governance

ecosystem in FY 2025-26. Suppliers representing over 90%

ernance

1.	
Brief outline on CSR policy of the company
	
The Company’s Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) 
initiatives are in the areas of Community Development, 
Skill Development and Road Safety. To create a visible 
and lasting impact, the Company focuses on a few CSR 
programmes rather than spreading resources thin over 
several projects.
	
Under the Community Development theme, the Company 
is committed to improving the well-being of the community 
by implementing social projects in designated villages 
around company’s

facilities and local communities. To 
create a positive and meaningful impact on the lives of 
communities, the projects are undertaken to strengthen 
the common community infrastructure and improve health, 
education, water, and sanitation services, ensuring all-
round development. Standout examples include a multi-
specialty tertiary care hospital and a modern CBSE school 
in Gujarat, and holistic village development initiatives 
targeting ultra-local problems in the designated villages, 
significantly improving the lives of local residents. In 
recent years, the Company has expanded its focus to 
address critical social priorities such as anemia reduction, 
promotion of menstrual hygiene among school children, 
large‑scale tree plantation, establishment of STEM 
laboratories, and development of school libraries.
	
The Company supports the measures to popularise the 
usage of Fermented Organic Manure (FOM) produced 
by biogas plants across India among the farmers. The 
project is implemented in phases including research on 
FOM, extension work comprising on-field demonstration 
& farmers connect program. Fermented Organic Manure 
(FOM) aligns with multiple SDGs and offers multiple 
benefits, including improved soil health, reduction in usage 
of chemical fertilisers, curb stubble burning, reduce the 
greenhouse gas emission, generate rural employment 
opportunities across the value chain, etc. contributing to 
sustainable agricultural development.
	
Through Skill Development initiatives, the Company focuses 
on skill development and employability enhancement of 
youth, aligned with industry requirements. As part of these 
initiatives, the company improves the quality of training, 
develops and upgrades training infrastructure including 
residential hostel facilities, facilitates holistic learning of 
students, through industry aligned curriculum as well as 
add-on courses, training of the trainers, and provides 
study material, scholarships, and practical traini

ng. 
The Japan India Institute for Manufacturing (JIM), the 
company’s flagship skill development institute, is a key 
institute for vocational skill development that trains the 
youth in vocational courses through the latest technology 
tools, industry exposure through on-the-job training and 
shop-floor practices based on Japanese manufacturing 
methods. The JIMs serve as centres of excellence and 
model ITI, preparing industry‑ready workforce for the 
manufacturing ecosystem. In addition to long‑term 
courses, the Company has recently introduced short‑term 
training programs aimed at upskilling the existing workforce 
through Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) and enhancing 
employment opportunities for youth through the Recruit, 
Train and Deploy (RTD) model. 
	
Beyond JIMs, the company upgrades selected government 
ITIs for manufacturing trades and automotive service 
trades. Through these initiatives, advanced labs are being 
set up, and industry relevant training is being provided 
to ITI trainers and students, aiming to build a workforce 
ready for the manufacturing industry. Ultimately, these 
interventions aim to progressively bring government ITIs 
at par with JIMs in terms of training quality, infrastructure, 
and industry relevance.
	
In the area of Road Safety, the company is dedicated 
to implementing the 5E approach, which encompasses 
Education, Evaluation, Enforcement, Engineering, and 
Emergency care. One of the most significant projects in 
the road safety area is the large-scale rollout of Automated 
Driving Test Tracks (ADTTs). ADTTs completely automate 
the driver license testing process, eliminating human 
bias and ensuring only the drivers with requisite skills 
receive the license. Additionally, in collaboration with 
State Governments, the company manages the Institute 
of Driving and Traffic Research (IDTRs) and Road 
Safety Knowledge Centers (RSKCs) to equip drivers 
with the necessary knowledge and skills. To strengthen 
traffic law

enforcement, the company also implements 
Integrated Traffic Safety Management System with real-
time monitoring and surveillance system to support law 
enforcement, surveillance and promote disciplined driving 
behaviour. To improve emergency care, the company also 
imparts first responder training to the commercial drivers 
and other stakeholders.
	
The Company encourages and recognises its employees 
for volunteering in the community by serving and sharing 
their expertise and skills to contribute to the local 
community development.

1. Background and EY’s Approach for the Impact 
Assessment
EY conducted an independent impact assessment of Maruti 
Suzuki India Limited’s (MSIL) CSR initiatives across the areas of 
Community Development, Skill Development, and Road Safety.
A combination of primary research (interviews, FGDs, surveys), 
field observations, and secondary analysis were used for the 
study. Given the nature of MSIL’s CSR portfolio, the assessment 
adopted a time-slice approach, which focuses on assessing the 
most relevant and observable outcomes at the current stage 
of a project’s lifecycle while recognising that long-term impact 
develops progressively over time.
Several interventions, including Village Development, 
Popularisation of FOM, Zydus Sitapur Hospital, Maruti Suzuki 
Podar Learn School, Japan India I

nstitute of Manufacturing (JIM), 
and ITI Upgradation programmes, are designed to drive long-
term systemic change. Accordingly, the assessment focused 
on foundational and intermediate outcomes such as improved 
access to services, increased service utilisation, institutional 
strengthening, and stakeholder confidence.
The assessment adopted a mixed-method approach, combining 
quantitative and qualitative techniques, with a strong emphasis 
on qualitative inquiry to capture stakeholder experiences, 
perceptions, and contextual factors. In-depth interviews, focus 
group discussions, and field observations complemented 
quantitative evidence to provide a comprehensive understanding 
of programme progress and outcomes. However, a significant 
proportion of the outcomes observed during the assessment 
were qualitative in nature, including enhanced community trust, 
behavioural changes, and improved workplace readiness.
The assessment also highlighted certain considerations related 
to outcome measurements across complex social development 
programmes. Several intended outcomes, such as reductions in 
road accidents, long-term livelihood improvements, enhanced 
educational attainment, and improved soil health, require 
sustained implementation and longer observation periods 
before they can be comprehensively assessed. In addition, 
outcomes such as behavioural change, trust, and community 
satisfaction remain inherently complex and often require 
qualitative approaches alongside conventional quantitative 
measurement techniques.
To complement traditional assessment methods, EY undertook 
an impact video documentation exercise across selected 
project locations. The exercise provided valuable insights 
into beneficiary experiences, community perspectives, and 
visible changes associated with programme implementation. 
It enabled the documentation of lived experiences, institutional 
improvements, and stakeholder perceptions that are often 
difficult to capture through q

uantitative indicators and served 
as an important visual record of programme outcomes and 
community impact.
The study also generated important learnings for strengthening 
future impact measurement
efforts. Going forward, impact assessments can be further 
strengthened through robust baseline studies, project-
specific outcome frameworks, periodic outcome tracking, 
and longitudinal monitoring of beneficiaries. As programmes 
continue to mature, future assessments may increasingly focus 
on measuring longer-term social, economic, and behavioural 
outcomes alongside indicators related to access, utilisation, 
and institutional strengthening.
Overall, the assessment indicates that MSIL’s CSR initiatives 
are contributing to stronger institutions, improved access to 
essential services, enhanced employability, and increased 
stakeholder confidence across project locations. The findings 
provide evidence of progress across the assessed interventions 
while highlighting the importance of continued monitoring, 
evaluation, and evidence generation to better understand 
and capture longer-term programme outcomes as these 
initiatives evolve.
2. Summary of Key Findings and Recommendations
MSIL’s CSR initiatives are driving system-level transformation 
and the impact created can be summarised under four 
dimensions: Access, Trust, Capability, and Dignity.
Access: MSIL’s CSR initiatives are expanding access to essential 
services and systems that were earlier limited by distance, 
infrastructure gaps, affordability, or process inefficiencies.
•	 Improved access to healthcare, education, water, sanitation, 
and village infrastructure, particularly in underserved rural 
and peri-urban locations.
•	 Strengthened access to industry-aligned skilling, 
apprenticeship, and vocational pathways for youth entering 
manufacturing and allied sectors.
•	 Expanded access to structured driver training and 
technology-enabled licence testing, making mobility systems 
more transparent and st

andardised.
Trust: The projects are strengthening trust by improving the 
quality, reliability, and fairness of public-facing services and 
community assets.
•	 Built community confidence in public infrastructure through 
better-quality assets, improved upkeep, and visible 
responsiveness to local needs.
•	 Enhanced employer confidence in trained youth by aligning 
curriculum, practical exposure, and certification with 
industry expectations.
•	 Improved trust in licensing and road safety systems through 
objective assessment, transparent processes, and reduced 
human discretion.
Capability: The initiatives are building individual, institutional, 
and community capability by combining infrastructure with 
knowledge, skills, and sustained support systems.
•	 Strengthened community capability through improved 
health awareness, education support, and better-functioning 
local institutions.
•	 Improved youth capability through hands-on technical 
training, workplace readiness, safety discipline, and exposure 
to real production environments.
•	 Built driver capability through structured training, simulator-
based practice, road safety education, and objective 
skill assessment.
Dignity: Across projects, dignity is being reinforced by 
improving everyday living conditions, enabling safer public 
services, and creating pathways for more secure livelihoods.
•	 Enhanced dignity in daily life through safe sanitation, 
reliable water access, improved public spaces, and better 
village infrastructure.
•	 Supported dignified livelihoods by improving employability, 
formal work exposure, and confidence among trainees 
and apprentices.
•	 Promoted safer and more responsible mobility behaviour, 
reinforcing dignity and accountability within road use and 
driver training systems.

1.	
Scope
1.1.	 This Nomination and Remuneration Policy (the “Policy”) 
has been framed in compliance with Section 178 of the 
Companies Act, 2013 (Act) and SEBI (Listing Obligations 
and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (‘Listing 
Regulations’).
1.2.	 This Policy aims to ensure that the persons appointed 
as Directors and Key Managerial Personnel (KMPs) as 
defined under the Act and Senior Management possess 
requisite qualifications, experience, expertise and 
attributes commensurate with their positions and level of 
management responsibilities and that the composition of 
remuneration to such persons is fair and reasonable and 
sufficient to attract, retain and motivate these persons to 
run the Company successfully.
1.3.	 This Policy is applicable to Directors, KMPs, Senior 
Management and other employees of the Company.
2.	
Objective
2.1.	 The objective of this Policy is to provide a framework for 
appointment, removal and remuneration of Directors, 
KMPs and Senior Management.
2.2.	 The Policy aims to provide:
	
(i)	
Criteria of appointment and removal of Directors, 
KMPs and Senior Management;
	
(ii)	
Criteria for determining qualifications, positive 
attributes and in

dependence of a Director;
	
(iii)	
Remuneration 
of 
Directors, 
KMPs 
and 
Senior Management;
	
(iv)	 Principles for retaining, motivating and promoting 
talent and ensuring long term retention of talent and 
creating competitive advantage.
3.	
Board Diversity
	
While considering the composition of the Board, the 
Nomination and Remuneration Committee (‘NRC’) will 
take into account the diversity of the members of the 
Board based on a number of factors, inter-alia, gender, 
age, qualifications, nationality, professional experience, 
recognition, skills and ability to add value to the business. 
Subject to the provisions of the Act including rules and 
regulations made thereunder and Listing Regulations, the 
Board shall have atleast one woman Director, persons 
who have strong technical/managerial/administrative

backgrounds relevant to the business of the Company and 
those who have excelled in one or more areas of finance/
accounting/law/public policy with top level administrative/
managerial experience.
4.	
Qualifications and Attributes for Directors, 
KMPs and Senior Management
4.1.	 The prospective Director:
	
(i)	
should be of the highest integrity and level of 
ethical standards;
	
(ii)	
should possess the requisite qualifications, skills, 
knowledge, experience and expertise relevant or 
useful to the business of the Company.
	
(iii)	
should, while acting as a Director be capable of 
balancing the interests of the Company, its employees, 
the shareholders, the community and of the need to 
ensure the protection of the environment; and
	
(iv)	 should inter-alia,
	
	
(a)	
uphold the highest ethical standards of integrity 
and probity;
	
	
(b)	
act objectively and constructively while 
exercising his/her duties;
	
	
(c)	
exercise his/her responsibilities in a bona fide 
manner in the interest of the Company;
	
	
(d)	
devote sufficient time and attention to his/
her professional obligations for inf

ormed and 
balanced decision making;
	
	
(e)	
not allow any extraneous considerations that will 
vitiate his/her exercise of objective independent 
judgment in the paramount interest of the 
Company as a whole, while concurring in or 
dissenting from the collective judgment of the 
Board in its decision making;
	
	
(f)	
not abuse his/her position to the detriment 
of the Company or its shareholders or other 
stakeholders or attempt to gain direct or 
indirect personal advantage or advantage for 
any associated person;
	
	
(g)	
avoid conflict of interest, and in case of any 
apparent situation of conflict of interest, make 
appropriate disclosures to the Board;
	
	
(h)	
assist the Company in implementing the best 
corporate governance practices;
	
	
(i)	
strictly adhere to and monitor legal compliances 
at all levels; and
	
	
(j)	
protect confidentiality of the confidential and 
proprietary information of the Company.
	
(v)	
In addition, in the case of an Independent Director(s), 
he/she must also satisfy the criteria specifically set 
out under applicable laws including the Act and the 
Listing Regulations.
4.2.	 The KMPs and the Senior Management should possess 
the highest integrity and ethical standards and have the 
requisite qualification and experience in any field relevant 
to and necessary for the business of the Company, 
including but not limited to technology, finance, law, public 
administration, management, accounting, marketing, 
production and human resource. They should also meet 
the requirements of the Act, Rules, Listing Regulations 
and/or any other applicable laws.
5.	
Evaluation of the Board, its Chairman, 
Individual Directors and Committees of the 
Board
	
The evaluation of the Board, its Chairman, individual 
Directors and committees of the Board shall be undertaken 
in compliance with the provisions of Section 134(3)(p), 
Section 178 and Listing Regulations.
6.	
Appointment and Removal of Non-Executive/
Independent Directors
6.1

Appointment
(i)	
Depending upon the requirements of the Company, the 
NRC shall identify from sources the Committee considers 
appropriate and reliable the persons who meet the 
requisite criteria and recommend their appointment to the 
Board at appropriate times.
(ii)	
The Board will consider the recommendations of the 
NRC and accordingly, approve the appointment and 
remuneration of Non-executive and/or Independent 
Directors, subject to the needs of the Company and the 
approval of the shareholders.
(iii)	
The appointment process shall be independent of the 
Company management. While selecting persons for 
appointment as Independent Directors, the Board shall 
ensure that there is an appropriate balance of skills, 
experience and knowledge in the Board so as to enable 
the Board to discharge its functions and duties effectively.
(iv)	 The appointment of Independent Directors shall be 
formalised by way of letters of appointment in accordance 
with the applicable laws and the requisite related 
disclosures in relation to such appointments made.
(v)	
The process for appointment of Independent Directors 
prescribed under the Act, the Listing Regulations and 
specifically the procedure set out under Schedule IV of 
the Act (Code for Independent Directors) will be followed. 
The Board shall also comply with other applicable laws.
6.2	 Removal
	
The appointment of an independent Director may be 
terminated at the recommendation of the NRC or by the 
Board on its own in the event he/she:
	
a.	
commits a breach of any of the duties, functions and 
responsibilities or obligations towards the Company 
or for reasons prescribed under the Act; or
	
b.	
compromises independence vis-à-vis the Company 
in any manner whatsoever which will have an impact 
on the criteria of independence.
	
c.	
If he/she becomes prohibited by law or under the 
Articles of Association from being an Independent 
Director of the Company.
7.	
Appointment and Removal of Managing 
Directo

r, Joint Managing Director, Whole- 
time Directors, KMPs and Senior Management 
Personnel
7.1.	 Appointment
(i)	
Depending upon the requirements of the Company for 
the above positions, the NRC shall identify persons and 
recommend their appointment to the Board including the 
terms of appointment and remuneration.
(ii)	
The Board will consider the recommendations of NRC and 
accordingly approve the appointment(s) and remuneration. 
The appointment of the Managing Director/Joint Managing 
Director/Whole-time Directors shall be subject to the 
approval of the shareholders.
(iii)	
The Managing Director shall have the power to finalise/
approve changes in Senior Management Personnel on 
account of routine/regular/annual internal promotions/
transfers in accordance with the HR Policy. However, new 
appointment as Senior Management Personnel will require 
approval of NRC/Board.
(iv)	 Appointments of other employees will be made in 
accordance with the Company’s Human Resource 
(HR) policy.
7.2.	 Removal
(i)	
The appointment of the Managing Director/Joint Managing 
Director/Whole-time Directors, may be terminated at the 
recommendation of the NRC or by the Board on its own, 
if such Director commits a breach of any of the duties,

8.	
Remuneration
8.1.	 The remuneration of the Non-executive/Independent 
Directors will include the following:
	
(i)	
Variable remuneration in the form of commission 
calculated as a percentage of the net profits of the 
Company as recommended by the NRC and to the 
extent permitted in the Act and approved by the 
Board and/or the shareholders of the Company. The 
payment of commission is based on criteria such as 
attendance at meetings of the Board/Committees of 
the Board, time devoted to the Company’s work, the 
responsibilities undertaken as Chairmen of various 
committees/the Board, their contribution to the 
conduct of the Company’s business, etc.
	
(ii)	
Sitting fee for attending meetings of the Board and 
committees constituted by the Board
	
(iii)	
Reimbursement of expenses for participation in the 
meetings of the Board and other meetings.
8.2.	 The remuneration of the Managing Director, Joint 
Managing Director, Whole-time Directors, KMPs and 
Senior Management Personnel should be commensurate 
with qualifications, experience and capabilities. The 
remuneration should take into account past performance 
and achievements and be in line with market standards. In 
determining the total remuneration, consideration should 
be given to the performance of the individual and also to the 
performance of the Company. In both cas

es, performance 
is measured against goals/plans determined beforehand 
at the commencement of a year and well communicated 
to the individual/the individual holding the management 
position, as the case may be.
8.3.	 The remuneration of the Managing Director/Joint Managing 
Director/Whole-time Directors/KMPs/Senior Management 
Personnel will include the following:
	
(i)	
Salary and allowances - fixed and variable besides 
other Benefits as per Rules contained in the HR 
Policy applicable to Senior Management Personnel;
	
(ii)	
Retirement benefits including provident fund/gratuity/
superannuation/leave encashment;
	
(iii)	
Performance linked bonus.
8.4.	 No Sitting Fee shall be payable to the Managing Director/
Whole-time Directors for attending meetings of Board or 
the committees constituted by the Board.
8.5.	 The remuneration of the employees other than Senior 
Management Personnel shall be as per Company’s 
HR Policy.
9.	
Increments
9.1.	 Increments of Managing Director/Joint Managing Director/
Whole-time Directors will be granted by the Board based 
on the recommendation of the NRC taking into account 
the performance of the individual, the performance of the 
business and the Company as a whole. Performance will 
be measured against pre- determined and agreed goals/
plans which are made known at the commencement of the 
year. The Board and the shareholders of the Company may

Corporate Governance Philosophy
Maruti Suzuki India Limited (the Company) is fully committed 
to practicing sound corporate governance and upholding the 
highest standards in conducting business. Being a value-driven 
organisation, the Company has always worked towards building 
trust with shareholders, employees, customers, suppliers and 
other stakeholders based on the principles of good corporate 
governance, viz., integrity, equity, transparency, fairness, 
disclosure, accountability and commitment to values. The 
Company fosters a culture in which high standards of ethical 
behaviour, individual accountability and transparent disclosure 
are ingrained in all of its business dealings and shared by its 
Board of Directors, Management and Employees. The Company 
has established systems and procedures to ensure that its 
Board of Directors is well-informed and well-equipped to fulfil 
its overall responsibilities and to provide the management with 
the strategic direction needed to create long-term shareholder 
value. Sustainable business practices are the foundation 
on which the Company operates since its inception.   The 
Company places utmost importance in creating value for all 
its stakeholders by actively promoting sustainable business 
practices across the value chain. The Company’s value creation 
principles are based on equitable, inclusive, transparent and 
collaborative stakeholder practices. The Company collaborates 
with the stakeholders to understand their needs and takes 
appropriate measures to address them.  Since inception, t

he 
Company has inculcated the 3R (Reduce-Reuse-Recycle) 
principles, Japanese practices and Suzuki Motor Corporation’s 
basic philosophy of ‘smaller, fewer, lighter, shorter and beauty’ 
in all its operating practices. These not only make the operations 
efficient but also support in resource optimisation leading 
to conservation of natural resources. The Company offers 
relevant products and technology that Indian customers need 
by leveraging the unique ability of Suzuki Motor Corporation 
to design feature-rich, safer, environment-friendly products 
with world class quality at an affordable price. The Company 
promotes a safe, healthy and happy workplace and always 
strives to be the employer of choice. The Company’s initiatives 
towards improving its Environmental, Social and Governance 
(ESG) performance and its contribution towards Sustainable 
Development Goals is placed in the Integrated Report.
Management Structure and Shared Leadership
The Company has a multi-tier management structure with 
the Board of Directors at the top.  The Company has various 
functions viz. Engineering, Product Planning, Quality Assurance, 
Corporate Governance Report
Production, Supply Chain, Marketing & Sales, Service, Parts & 
Accessories, Finance, Company Secretary, Legal, Corporate 
Planning, Corporate Affairs, Information Technology, Digital 
Enterprise and Human Resource. The Managing Director & CEO 
is supported by Member Executive Committee (MECs) in setting 
strategic direction for the Company. The board meetings of the 
Company mark the presence of Senior Management Personnel, 
as may be required, as they act as a channel between the Board 
above them and the employees. This structure not only allows 
easy and quick communication of field information to the Board 
members but also gives the top management the opportunity 
to give recommendations relevant to their business operations.
Through this, it is ensured that:
•	 Strategic supervision is provided by the Board;
•

Control and implementation of the Company’s strategy is 
achieved effectively;
•	 Operational management remains focused on implementation;
•	 Information regarding the Company’s operations and 
financial performance are made available adequately;
•	 Delegation of decision making with accountability is achieved;
•	 Financial and operating controls are maintained at an optimal 
level; and
•	 Risk is suitably evaluated and dealt with.

CEO/CFO Certification
The Company has institutionalised the framework for CEO/CFO certification by establishing a transparent “controls self-
assessment” mechanism, thereby laying the foundation for development of the best corporate governance practices which are 
vital for a successful business. It is the Company’s endeavour to attain the highest level of governance to enhance the stakeholders’ 
value. To enable certification by CEO/CFO for the financial year 2025-2026, key controls over financial reporting were identified and 
subjected to self-assessment by control owners in the form of completion of self-assessment questionnaires through a web based 
online tool called “Controls Manager”. The self-assessments submitted by control owners were further reviewed and approved 
by their superiors and the results of the self-assessment process were presented to the auditors and the audit committee. The 
whole exercise was carried out in an objective manner to assess the effectiveness of internal financial controls including controls 
over financial reporting during the financial year 2025-2026.

Commodities Price Risk Management and Hedge 
Policy
1.0	 Background
Maruti Suzuki India Limited (MSIL) for producing cars needs 
to purchase large volumes of basic commodities like steel, 
aluminium directly and indirectly and con

sume high quantities 
of copper and lead being used by its vendors for supplying 
components. Apart from these basic metals, significant 
quantities of Precious Group Metals like Platinum, Palladium 
and Rhodium as well as other commodities like plastics, High 
speed diesel (HSD) etc., are consumed.
Due to high volume usage of the above-mentioned commodities 
in manufacturing cars and very high price volatility, which is 
being witnessed in last couple of years, Company is exposed 
to severe commodity price risk directly as well as indirectly. 
These commodities are either being purchased from suppliers 
directly at mutually negotiated rates or the price is settled with 
suppliers, who manufacture these components for MSIL using 
these commodities, at monthly/quarterly settled prices based 
on prevalent market trends.
Since these commodities and components are not purchased 
under a fixed price contract, the cost of the raw material input 
is variable.
2.0	 Commodities 
Price 
Risk 
Management 
Objective and Strategies
The commodities price risk management objective of the 
Company is to hedge the risk of changes in the commodity prices 
procured directly or indirectly (i.e., procured by component 
supplier). Since the fluctuations in commodity prices have 
severe impact on financials of the Company, hedging provides 
stability to the financial performance by estimating the amount 
of future cash flows and reducing volatility.
The Company shall follow a consistent policy of mitigating the 
commodities price risk by undertaking following strategies:
I.	
Bundling of commodity sourcing
	
Under this strategy, the Company shall negotiate with 
suppliers bundling its in house requirement with its vendor 
requirement to get a better price for different commodities 
based on large consolidated volume.
II.	
Bundling of Suzuki Motor Corporation’s (SMC )
subsidiaries sourcing
	
This strategy allows the Company to bundle the commodity 
sourcing for the SMC subsidiaries prese

nt in India in order 
to get better pricing for all the SMC group companies 
in India.
III.	 Commodity Grade Standardisation & Substitution
	
The Company shall undertake grade standardisation 
across various categories of commodities to the extent 
possible like in the case of steel and plastic products so 
as to optimise the costs.
	
The Company shall also change raw material grades to 
cheaper grades without affecting product performance 
e.g. in the case of steel from IF to EDD grade.
IV.	 Yield Improvement
	
The Company shall continuously under take yield 
improvement activities across various commodities like in 
the case of plastic products and electrical components, 
etc., done so far.
V.	
Commodity price risk hedging
	
MSIL shall follow a consistent policy of mitigating 
commodities price risk by entering into appropriate 
hedging instruments as considered necessary from time 
to time. Depending on the future outlook on commodity 
prices, the Company may keep the exposures un-hedged 
or hedge only a part of the total exposure.
	
The Company shall not enter into commodity hedging 
transactions for speculative purposes i.e. without any 
actual/anticipated underlying exposure.
	
The Company shall strictly observe the rules and regulations 
laid down by RBI for undertaking the commodities price 
risk hedging.
3.0	 Commodities Permitted for Hedging
The Company may hedge commodities price risk on all the 
commodities being purchased directly or indirectly e.g. 
Aluminium, Copper, Lead, Platinum, Rhodium, Palladium, 
Steel, Plastic, etc., wherever possible and permissible under 
the applicable rules and regulations to enable fixing the 
sourcing costs.

Overview
In FY 2025-26, the Indian economy demonstrated remarkable 
resilience and outperformed expectations despite heightened 
geopolitical risk, which led to supply challenges and a rise in trade 
protectionist measures across several countries. In this context, the 
Government of India and the RBI prioritised strengthening domestic 
economic activities to of

fset risks to exports.
The government introduced a range of measures to stimulate 
domestic consumption, fast-track investment and support 
employment, including GST reform, personal income tax relief, front-
loaded capital expenditure, and enhanced credit support to MSMEs. 
At the same time, benign inflation provided the RBI with room to 
reduce interest rates and support economic growth. Besides, RBI’s 
astute liquidity management for quicker transmission of policy rate 
cuts and efforts to contain volatility in forex market were noteworthy.
However, towards the end of the year, the West Asia conflict created 
supply and cost shocks that weighed on economic momentum and 
led to a sharp depreciation of the rupee against the US dollar. Going 
forward, the effect of geopolitical tensions on economy may likely 
prevail. In addition, the risk of an El Niño-induced weak monsoon 
is emerging.

Industry Overview and Annual Summary
India retained its position as the third-largest passenger vehicle (PV) 
market globally, with sales of around 4.7 million units in FY 2025-26, 
registering a growth of around 8% y-o-y over FY 2024-25.
However, the yearly growth figure does not convey the underlying 
demand environment that prevailed over the entire year. FY 2025-26 
can be best described as a ‘year of two halves’. The year started with 
a subdued demand environment, leading to a decline of 0.4% y-o-y in 
the first half, followed by a sharp recovery, with growth accelerating to 
16.7% y-o-y in the second half. Recovery in the second half was aided 
by GST reforms, which revived demand in the small car segment, 
falling under the lower 18% GST bracket. Such a meaningful reduction 
in indirect taxes in a single stroke is relatively uncommon.
Since FY 2018-19, the small car segment, especially entry-level 
cars, has witnessed significant contraction in demand, due to 
price in

creases driven mainly by regulatory changes. As a result, a 
significant portion of customers who traditionally opted for entry-level 
cars were priced out of the market. This structural shift constrained 
overall industry growth, which grew below its potential at around 4.3% 
CAGR between FY 2018-19 and FY 2024-25. The demand expansion 
largely concentrated in higher-priced segments.
The GST reform acted as a key inflection point, improving affordability 
and triggering a revival in demand, especially for small cars. This 
recovery is significant, given the segment’s critical role in driving first-
time buyers and expanding overall market size. While the recovery 
in small cars supported broader demand revival, SUVs continued to 
support industry growth, maintaining a dominant share of overall PV 
sales. SUVs continued to account for over 56% of PV sales.

made six airbags and Electronic Stability Control as a standard 
in nearly 100% of its product portfolio, the only OEM in the 
country to offer such safety features as standard across a wide 
and diverse portfolio. The Company's fleet is fully compliant 
with key Indian emission and safety regulations, including the 
Corporate Average Fuel Economy (CAFE Phase 2).

Management Discussion and Analysis
Design for Recycling
With the objective of preventing vehicles from being discarded 
as waste at the end of their useful life, the Company continues 
to design vehicles for maximum recyclability and recoverability. 
Design decisions are guided by the principle of maximising 
resource circulation, thereby reducing dependence on virgin 
resources and supporting a circular economy.
Currently, the materials used in all vehicles manufactured by 
the Company are at least 92% recyclable and 99% recoverable 
at the end of their useful life (ELV). These levels exceed the 
recyclability and recoverability thresholds prescribed under the 
European Union's End-of-Life Vehicle (EU-ELV) framework.
Promoting Circular Economy through the 3R 
Principle
The Company actively promotes circular economy principles 
through the 3R (Reduce, Reuse and Recycle) approach, helping 
conserve natural resources, minimise waste generation and 
improve resource productivity across operations. The Company 
recycles 100% of the metallic scrap generated during vehicle 
manufacturing and continuously undertakes yield-improvement

initiatives to optimise the use of raw materials such as steel and 
aluminium.  
Water conservation remains a key focus area. The Company 
recycles 100% of its used water and meets nearly two-thirds 
of manufacturing requirements through recycled water and 
rainwater harvesting. During the year, the Company further 
strengthened its water stewardship efforts and secured Water 
Positivity certification at both its Gurugram and Manesar facilities, 
achieving water positivity indices of 1.90 and 1.23, respectively. 
These achievements are particularly significant as both facilities 
are located in water-stressed regions. The other two facilities in 
Kharkhoda, Haryana and Hansalpur, Gujarat, do not fall under 
water-stressed region. 
To encourage material recycling, the Maruti Suzuki and Toyota 
Tsusho Group’s Vehicle Scrapping and Recycling unit began 
operations in 2021. The facility provides an easy, eco-friendly 
solution for customers to scrap vehicles with a capacity to scrap 
24,000 vehicles annually.
To reduce plastic packaging consumption, it has adopted the 
‘Eliminate-Alternate-Reduce’ (EAR) strategy, with over 20% of 
packaging material for Knocked Down (KD) kits and components 
being reused. In FY 2025-26, the Company enabled the recycling 
of more than 2,819 MT of packaging plastic.
Additionally, the Company has implemented Extended Producer 
Responsibility programmes to recycle plastic packaging used in 
aftermarket parts and accessories and e-waste.
The Company also continues to reduce the environmental impact 
of logistics operations by increasing the use of rail transportation 
for vehicle dispatches, thereby reducing fuel consumption and 
associated greenhouse gas emissions. 
Low-Carbon Energy Transition and Sustainable 
Manufacturing
The Company continues to pursue a structured low-
carbon energy transition pathway to reduce emissions from 
manufacturing operations. While usage of renewable electricity 
remains an important pillar of this strategy,

the Company is also 
actively working towards decarbonising process emissions in 
manufacturing operations, which currently use fossil fuels like 
CNG/Propane.
The Company is expanding renewable electricity use through 
in-house solar plants and green power purchases (solar and 
hybrid power). It is also shifting, in the long term, to low-carbon 
fuels by replacing fossil CNG with Compressed Biogas and 
exploring Green Hydrogen for manufacturing.
Environment Protection
The Company not only complies with applicable environmental 
laws and regulations but also strives to surpass them through 
robust environmental management systems across the 
product lifecycle. This includes a well-established framework 
for controlling the usage of Substances of Concern (SoCs) in 
products through globally recognised International Material 
Data System (IMDS) at the product development stage to 
systematically review and monitor the material composition 
of parts and components. These efforts are supported by the 
Company's green procurement guidelines.
The Company also continues to adopt environmentally 
responsible waste management practices and has maintained

Pursuing Multi-Powertrain Technology Strategy – 
Maximising Reduction of Carbon Footprint of the 
Fleet
The Company remains committed to supporting India's carbon 
Net Zero ambition while ensuring mobility solutions that are 
relevant to a broad customer base. In the automobile industry, 
the product use phase accounts for the largest share of 
lifecycle carbon emissions. Consequently, reducing emissions 
from products remains a key engineering priority for the 
Company. Through sustained focus on efficiency improvement, 
deployment of lower-emission technologies, and adoption of 
alternate fuel and powertrain technologies, the Company’s 
average CO2 emission of its fleet is significantly lower than 
the industry average. Not only that, but the Company has also 
been outperforming its CAFE target by a wide margin in both 
phase 1 (2017-2022) and phase 2 (2023-ongoing). 
Recognising that meaningful carbon reduction requires every 
vehicle sold to contribute, the Company believes that India's 
transition towards lower-carbon mobility will require multiple 
technology pathways. For a large and diverse market such as 
India, where affordability remains a key consideration and per 
capita income levels are lower than those in developed markets, a 
single technology solution may not adequately address customer 
needs. Therefore, the Company continues to pursue a multi-
pathway strategy that combines Battery Electric Vehicles, Strong 
Hybrid Electric Vehicles, vehicles powered with CNG/Compressed 
Biogas (CBG), gasoline vehicles compatible with 20% ethanol 
blending, and Flex Fuel Vehicle technologies. This approach seeks 
to reduce emissions while preserving affordability, customer 
choice, energy security and suitability to local resource availability.
During the year, the Company launched e VITARA, its first 
Battery Electric Vehicle. Whi

le Battery Electric Vehicles remain 
an important component of future mobility, the Company 
continues to advance multiple technologies to accelerate fleet-
wide carbon reduction.

Management Discussion and Analysis
Supply Chain Management
The automotive manufacturing supply chain is inherently complex 
and geographically dispersed, with deep interdependencies 
across multiple tiers of suppliers. The Company's supply 
ecosystem comprises nearly 450 Tier-1 suppliers and about 
1,500 Tier-2 suppliers, collectively supporting the production 
of nearly 2.5 million vehicles annually. In an increasingly 
interconnected global environment, supply chains are being 
influenced by geopolitical developments and evolving trade 
regulations, creating uncertainties around material availability 
and heightened cost volatility.
During the year, global supply chains experienced disruptions 
arising f

rom rare earth export restrictions, highlighting 
vulnerabilities associated with critical materials and globally 
concentrated supply bases. Towards the close of the financial 
year, developments in the Middle East further heightened supply 
chain risks as disruptions in critical inputs such as natural gas 
and petroleum, among others, began impacting global supply 
chains, contributing to higher energy and logistics costs. For 
an organisation operating one of India's largest automotive 
supplier ecosystems, the challenge extended beyond its 
own operations to ensuring stability across the entire value 
chain. Working proactively with suppliers across all tiers, the 
Company undertook timely interventions to ensure continuity 
of operations.
Against this backdrop, the Company remained focused on 
strengthening supply chain resilience, enhancing localisation 
and mitigating supply risks. At the same time, it continued to 
work closely with suppliers across the value chain to build the 
capacity, capability and competitiveness required to support 
its ambition of scaling production to 4 million units per annum 
by FY 2030-31.
